The Long Game Part III: Theory and Exploitation

Chapter 26 Preliminary draft

Tells, Table Talk, and Table Presence

Physical and verbal tells, how reliable they are, and your own image.

A tell is a habit that leaks information, and most of them leak less than movies suggest. This chapter shows you what to watch, how to rank what you see, how to turn a read into a number you can act on, and how to manage what others see in you.

A tell is a tendency, not a fact

A tell is any behavior that shows a little about a player's hand or intentions: a glance, a pause, a sentence, the way chips move. Live poker gives you these for free. Online players cannot see each other, but at a live $2/$5 table you sit three feet from the person you are playing.

The key word is tendency. A tell does not say what a player holds. It says that, for this player, a hand of this kind is a little more or a little less likely. Treat it like a hunch you can count. This chapter makes a judgment-based case: we rank tells by how much they seem to tell you, in our judgment as a study book, and we cite no studies. Your own notes on your own opponents beat any list printed here.

Most tells come in two sorts. A reliable-in-context tell works because a player is relaxed and does not know about it. An acted tell is a show put on for you, and the people who put on shows often want you to guess wrong. The second sort is the reason a tell must be compared with the same player's baseline, meaning how that person acts when nothing is at stake.

What Daniel Negreanu might say

He would say that reads are the heart of live play, but that the best ones come from putting together bet sizes, timing, and what a player has shown before, not from a single twitch. He would also remind you that the same read can be wrong the next hour.

An imagined voice: our reading of Negreanu's public emphasis on hand reading, not his words.

Physical and timing tells

Start with what you can see without staring. Watch the hands, the chips, and the clock.

Timing. How long a player takes before acting is the easiest signal to collect. The rule is to compare each action with that player's usual pace. A recreational player who snap-calls a flop bet is often holding a hand he does not want to think about, such as a medium pair or a draw. A long, showy pause followed by a bet or raise is often a strong hand acting unsure, because a player who is bluffing rarely wants to draw attention to himself. A long pause before a fold usually means only that he wanted to continue and could not. In most low-stakes live games, a sudden break from a player's own normal speed is worth more than the speed itself.

Chip handling. Watch who the motion is aimed at. A player who quietly readies chips before his turn, while not watching you, has usually already decided to bet or call. A player who grabs chips as you reach for yours, while watching you, is often putting on a show to stop your bet, and in most low-stakes live games that leans toward a weak or medium hand. A neat stack set out for a bet can differ from a handful grabbed without counting. A player who glances at his own stack right after the flop often likes the flop and is planning a bet. These are habits of timing and intent, not hands.

Hands and body. Shaking hands on a big bet mean adrenaline. In most low-stakes live games that leans toward a strong hand: the release of tension after a player makes a big hand is hard to hide, while a bluffer is usually working hard to keep still. It is not certain, because a nervous new player can shake with anything. Many players freeze, sit very still, and breathe shallowly when bluffing, because they fear any motion will give them away. A player who protects his cards early and then forgets them may be showing his interest in the hand.

Keep the notes short and tied to a number you can check later. "Reaches for chips early" means little. "Reached early on three bets, held a set, a flush, and a bluff" means the habit did not separate strong hands from weak ones, and you should not use it.

Table talk and how reliable tells are

Table talk is anything said during a hand: a joke, a question, a comment about the board, a direct "what do you have?" Live players talk a lot, and talk is cheap, so it is also the easiest to fake. Still, speech has three uses.

  • Change in talk. A chatty player who goes silent after a bet has changed his baseline. A quiet player who suddenly speaks has too. The change counts more than the words.
  • What the words are about. Players who say "I cannot beat anything" while putting chips in are often trying to tempt a call. Players who say nothing are often trying to avoid saying the wrong thing. Both are guesses, and we call them guesses.
  • Reactions to your talk. If you ask a question and he answers fast and easily, then looks away, that can mean more than what he said. Do not overdo it. Many players find constant questions rude, and the dealer may step in. See Appendix F, Live Etiquette and House Rules for the house rules on talk and showing cards.

Here is the ranking promised in the lead. Nothing here is measured. It is our judgment, built on how often each signal appears and how clearly it separates strong hands from weak ones. Move any point you disagree with after a month of your own notes.

What David Sklansky might say

He would say that tells are a small, noisy input and that most players overpay for them. His reasoning in The Theory of Poker is about mistakes and expected value: start from the numbers, and let a read move you only when the hand is close.

An imagined voice: our reading of the ideas in The Theory of Poker, not his words.

Weighing a tell as evidence

This is the hard part. A tell does not tell you what he holds. It moves a probability, and sometimes that is enough to turn a fold into a call. Here is a worked example with real money.

The river is out, the pot is $200, and a villain bets $100, half the pot. You hold a bluff-catcher, a hand that beats only a bluff. You risk $100 to win $300. node tools/poker.js odds 200 100 says you need 25% equity, so you must be beating a bluff at least 25% of the time.

Call needs: 100 / (200 + 100 + 100) = 100 / 400 = 25%

From his history you judge that in this spot he bluffs 20 times out of 100 bets and values the rest. That is below 25%, so with no read you fold. Now suppose you have watched him all night and noticed one habit: after a bet he stares at you. Over many bets you judge that he stares on about 60% of his bluffs and about 15% of his value bets. These two numbers are guesses, and the whole result depends on them.

Of the 24 bets with a stare, 12 are bluffs. That is 12 / 24 = 50%, well above the 25% you need. Of the 76 bets with no stare, 8 are bluffs, 8 / 76 = 10.5%, so you fold. The tell moved the same hand from a fold to a call at 50%, and made the no-stare fold clearer.

A single read is worth this much only when the two rates (60% and 15%) are good. Change them and the answer changes. The table below shows how much a tell moves a prior, depending on how strong the tell is. The number "tell strength" is a likelihood ratio: how many times more likely the signal is with a bluff than with a value bet. In our example it is 0.60 / 0.15 = 4.

Read the table across a row. A 10% prior needs a 3x tell just to reach the 25% line, and a 4x tell gets it only to 30.8%. A signal at 1.5x on a 20% prior reaches 27.3%, which is a call, but only just, and a small error in your guess flips it. This is why we say a tell is evidence, not proof. Use it when the hand was already close.

Key idea

A tell changes your estimate. It does not replace it. If the hand was already clear without it, the tell should not change what you do.

The pot is $200 and he bets $100. With no read you think he bluffs 20% of the time. He taps his chips before betting, which you judge twice as likely with a bluff as with a value bet. Does your estimate cross 25%, and what if the tap were half as likely with a bluff?

Prior odds 0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25. Times 2 is 0.50, and 0.50 / 1.50 = 33.3%, past the 25% line, so you call. Half as likely: 0.25 x 0.5 = 0.125, and 0.125 / 1.125 = 11.1%, so you fold with more confidence.

Why is a tell worth less when your prior is 10% than when it is 40%?

A tell multiplies odds. At 10% the odds are 0.11 to 1, so doubling them gives 0.22 and only 18.2%. At 40% the odds are 0.67, and doubling gives 1.33, or 57.1%. The same tell moves a middling prior much further than a tiny one. This is why you should not hero-call on a hunch when the player almost never bluffs.

For the broader method of finding where an opponent deviates, see Chapter 24, Exploitative Play, and see Chapter 19, Hand Reading for building the range the tell is moving.

Your own image and presence

Everything above works in reverse. The other eight players are reading you, and some of them are better at it than you are. Your image is the picture they hold of how you play, built from the hands you showed and the way you behaved. It has two layers: what you do in hands (tight, loose, aggressive), and how you carry yourself (calm, talkative, nervous).

The first layer is the one that pays. If you have shown down only strong hands for two hours, a bet from you looks strong, and a bluff gets more folds. If you have been caught three times with weak hands, a bet looks weak and good hands get paid. Neither image is better in itself. An image is a tool, and you can use it against particular opponents. See Chapter 25, Live Player Types and Population Tendencies for which players pay attention to it, and Chapter 18, Bluffing and Semi-Bluffing for when a bluff is a good idea at all.

The second layer, how you carry yourself, is about not giving away more than you mean to. Players who want to be hard to read work on a few habits.

What Phil Ivey might say

He would point to total focus and a presence that gives nothing away. He would say the goal is not a mask but a habit that never changes, so there is nothing to find.

An imagined voice: our reading of how Ivey is publicly described, as a focused, hard-to-read player, not his words.

Do not confuse presence with rudeness. You can be friendly, steady, and unreadable at once. Slowing a hand to look for a tell is fine. Holding up the game for a minute at every decision is not, and it makes the table less willing to talk, which costs you reads. A good live player keeps the game pleasant, because a pleasant table is a talkative one, and a talkative one leaks.

Table Math

Weight a tell as evidence, not proof

The shortcut. Multiply the odds, not the percentage. Turn your prior into odds (20% is 1 to 4), multiply by how many times more likely the tell is with a bluff than with value, then turn it back.

Prior 20% = 0.25 odds. Tell is 4 times as likely with a bluff: 0.25 x 4 = 1.00 odds = 50%

Where it bends. The tell strength is a guess, and a small error in it moves the answer. A 2x tell on a 20% prior gives 33.3%, but a 1.5x tell gives 27.3%, and both are only a little past the 25% a half-pot bet asks. If the call is close in either direction, treat the tell as a tiebreaker. If you cannot say how often the tell shows up with value hands, you do not know its strength.
